Tools, Materials, and the Job Inventory

Unit 1: Field Planning. Lesson 6 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

A forklift drops a pallet at the loading dock and the driver wants a signature now. Whoever signs owns what is on that pallet, so the check starts before the pen.

Materials against the drawings

Your materials list comes from the drawings: how many outlets, how many jacks, how many feet of cable, how many boxes and supports. Inventory the supplies against that list. If a count looks low, tell the foreman while there is still time to order.

Checking a delivery

Check             What you look for
Part number       matches the order and the materials list
Category          printed on the box and the jacket, as ordered
Listing           the right rating for the space: CMP, CMR, CM
Quantity          the count and the footage, not just the box count
Damage            crushed boxes, kinked cable, wet cartons

Note damage on the delivery slip before you sign. Move the material to the staging space, off the floor if it can get wet, and keep it where the crew can find it and strangers cannot.

Installer hand tools

  • Strippers remove the jacket without nicking the conductors.
  • Punch-down tool seats and trims wire on an IDC.
  • Crimper attaches modular plugs and some connectors.
  • Fish tape pulls a string through a wall or conduit.
  • Label maker prints durable labels.
  • Cable tester checks wiremap before you leave the room.
  • Ladder: inspect it before each use.

Keep blades sharp and clean. A dull blade nicks a conductor and a dirty one leaves a mess in a jack.

Track the footage

Cable reels carry footage marks. Write the starting and ending mark for each cable on your pull sheet, so waste is visible and a short pull is caught before a reel runs out.

Tip: never leave a reel exposed overnight where weather or other trades can damage it.
Exam tip: the FIRST step when a delivery arrives is to check it against the materials list and the order, then note any damage before signing.
Remember
Check every delivery for part number, category, listing, quantity, and damage before you sign, then stage it and track the footage.
Deeper explanation

Tools, Materials, and the Job Inventory, explained slowly

A delivery check, step by step

A good installer treats a delivery the way a pharmacist treats a prescription: check it before accepting it. A fast, written check prevents most installation delays.

Order line            Delivered           Result
Category 6 box, 4     4 boxes             match
Category 6A box, 2    1 box               short; note on slip
CMP rating, 2 boxes   2 boxes, CMR print  wrong listing; reject
Jacks, 100            100                 match
J-hooks, 200          190, 3 bent         short and damaged; note

The CMP versus CMR line is the dangerous one. The box says one thing and the jacket says another, so you open a reel and read the jacket. A riser cable cannot go in a plenum ceiling.

Materials against the drawings

Count from the drawings: if the plan shows 80 outlets, you need at least 80 jacks plus spares, 80 faceplates, and enough cable for 80 routes plus slack. Compute cable by route length, not by hope. For 80 drops at an average of 55 m, you need 80 x 55 = 4400 m, which is about 14 400 ft. Add waste and slack, and compare with the delivered footage.

Tool care

  • Strippers: blades sharp, set for the cable's jacket, never for a different one.
  • Punch-down tool: blade seated and the right type for the block.
  • Crimper: dies matched to the plug.
  • Label maker: fresh tape and a clean head.
  • Tester: batteries charged, adapters clean, reference done at the start of the session.
  • Ladder: inspected each day.

Staging

Stage materials in the work area or a locked cage. Keep reels covered and off a wet floor. Keep boxes labeled with the room or the pull. A crew spends less time searching when staging follows the drawings.

Remember: check, count, note damage before you sign, and track footage from the first cut to the last.
